01 · Grid profile: can EIA-930 carry an hourly day-ahead study, and what does Utah's rush hour look like?¶

Question. Before we forecast anything, is the public EIA-930 grid data complete and clean enough for an hourly, day-ahead "traffic report"? What must be cleaned or excluded, when is Utah's (PACE's) rush hour, how good is each balancing authority's (BA's) own day-ahead forecast as a baseline, and which ~10 BAs should the overview use?

Short answer.

  • Coverage is excellent from 2019 for the recommended BAs: demand is reported in at least 99.75 % of hours.
  • EIA's "adjusted" demand still contains isolated spikes, and most hours EIA imputed are an exact copy of the BA's own forecast. Spikes are removed, and imputed hours are never scored.
  • PACE's rush hour is narrow: a few dozen summer late-afternoon hours a year.
  • The BA's own forecast is a strong baseline for most BAs (PACE: 4.0 % error), but two BAs publish it an hour off, and it can never be an input to a day-ahead model, because it is published on the day it forecasts.

How to read this notebook. Every number below is recomputed from the cached EIA-930 snapshot by importing lab/scripts/recon_grid.py, the code behind docs/data-profile/grid.md. Values are observed (EIA-930 as published) unless a label says modeled. Times are UTC unless a column says local.

Seal. The sealed test window [2025-11-01Z, 2026-11-01Z) appears once, in §1.2, as row counts and missing hours only. Everything else passes through gridpilot.splits.drop_sealed first.

0. Setup and inputs¶

The recon module is imported with its outputs redirected to a scratch directory (gridpilot.notebook.import_recon), so this notebook never rewrites the committed profile figures. The input table is pinned by its sha256, which must match the snapshot the profile cites.

In [1]:
import json
import shutil
import tempfile
from datetime import UTC, datetime
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import polars as pl

from gridpilot import notebook as nb
from gridpilot.paths import MANIFEST_DIR
from gridpilot.splits import TEST_START, drop_sealed

nb.setup()
SCRATCH = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="nb01_"))
rg = nb.import_recon("recon_grid", SCRATCH)


def table(name: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    # Tables that recon_grid wrote to the scratch directory.
    return pl.read_csv(SCRATCH / f"{name}.csv")


CORE = ["PACE", "CISO", "BPAT", "AZPS", "NEVP", "PSCO", "ERCO", "SWPP", "MISO", "PJM"]
OPTIONAL = ["IPCO", "NYIS"]

1. Coverage¶

1.1 Before the seal (2019-01 to 2025-10)¶

The heatmap below has one row per BA (grouped by EIA region) and one column per month. A cell is dark blue when the BA reported demand in nearly every hour of that month, and pale when hours are missing. Values below 80 % are clipped to the palest colour. The first UTC hours of 2019 are missing for every BA (they sit in a 2018 file we did not download), which is why January 2019 is never quite full.

1.2 Sealed window: completeness only¶

For the sealed window we look only at counts: how many rows each BA has, and how many hours lack demand or the DF, up to the last full day before retrieval (2026-10-25). No value from the window is read. Every candidate BA has all 8,592 expected rows. The window will end at the frozen snapshot's availability cutoff, and results will state the days they cover.

Two completeness facts that matter for the design.

  • WACM and WAUW have only about 3,630 of 8,592 rows, and SWPW and BHBA about 4,960: the two old BAs stop and the two new ones start around 2026-04-01, inside the window. WACM is PACE's largest import neighbour, so anything built on interchange must handle the switch, and the core region set leaves these BAs out.
  • PACE's DF runs past its last reported demand hour (the count above): EIA publishes the forecast for "today" while demand for today is still arriving. That is the publication pattern behind §4's rule that the DF cannot be a model input.

2. Cleaning rules¶

Three rules, each with the number of hours it touches:

  1. Use EIA's adjusted demand, not the raw column. Where EIA replaced a reported value, the raw value was absurd (unit or keying errors).
  2. Remove isolated spikes. EIA's adjustment keeps some single-hour spikes. Rule: an hour more than 15 % away from the mean of its two neighbours, while the neighbours agree within 10 %. Flagged hours (and values ≤ 0) are nulled in demand_clean_mw.
  3. Never score on imputed hours. EIA fills missing demand first with the BA's own forecast, so imputed hours mostly equal the DF and would flatter that baseline.

The PACE example from the profile: on 2021-09-13 at 21Z, PACE reported 12,566 MW while generation minus interchange (NG − TI) was about 6,500 MW, and the hours either side agree with each other.

Why the spike rule matters. One bad hour sets a fake annual peak, and then almost no real hour is "near the peak": the rush-hour count for PACE in 2021 collapses from 40 hours to 1. Every peak statistic below uses the cleaned series.

imp = pre.filter(pl.col("ba").is_in(rg.CANDIDATES) & pl.col("demand_imputed"))
copies = imp.filter(pl.col("demand_adj_mw") == pl.col("demand_forecast_mw"))

1,181 imputed candidate-BA demand hours; 996 of them equal the BA's DF exactly (84%).

The imputation leak. If imputed hours were scored, the BA's forecast would be graded against a copy of itself on those hours: zero error by construction. The table isolates that effect for the BAs with at least 20 imputed hours (2019-01 to 2025-10). Both error columns exclude spike hours; the first also keeps the imputed hours, the second drops them. Keeping them always makes the baseline look better. The effect is small because imputed hours are rare (largest for FPL: 4.19 % instead of 4.24 %), but it is one-sided, and the same hours would contaminate any model trained on the adjusted series.

In [12]:
pe = (pl.col("demand_forecast_mw") - pl.col("demand_adj_mw")).abs() / pl.col("demand_adj_mw")
ok = (pl.col("demand_forecast_mw") > 0) & (pl.col("demand_adj_mw") > 0) & ~pl.col("d_spike")
leak = (pre.filter(pl.col("ba").is_in(rg.CANDIDATES) & ok)
        .group_by("ba").agg(
            pl.col("demand_imputed").sum().alias("imputed_h"),
            (pl.col("demand_imputed") & (pl.col("demand_adj_mw") == pl.col("demand_forecast_mw"))).sum()
            .alias("imputed_h_equal_to_DF"),
            (pe.mean() * 100).round(3).alias("DF_MAPE_with_imputed_h_%"),
            (pe.filter(~pl.col("demand_imputed")).mean() * 100).round(3).alias("DF_MAPE_scored_h_only_%"))
        .filter(pl.col("imputed_h") >= 20).sort("imputed_h", descending=True))

3. Rush-hour structure¶

The small multiples show the average day in the validation year (2024-11 to 2025-10), in local time, for summer (orange) and winter (blue). Solid lines are demand; dashed lines are net load, demand minus wind and solar, which is what the rest of the fleet must cover. Each curve is divided by the BA's annual mean demand, so 1.0 is an average hour.

In [13]:
rg.rush_hour(pre)
nb.show(SCRATCH / "daily_profiles.png")

What the figure shows. PACE's summer demand peaks at 17:00 local, but its net load peaks at 20:00, after the sun sets on Utah's solar. Solar-heavy BAs (CISO, NEVP, AZPS) have deep midday net-load troughs and steep evening ramps. BPAT is the odd one out: it peaks on winter mornings.

How concentrated is the rush hour? The next figure counts, for each BA, the hours per year within 5 % of that year's peak (median of 2019–2024), for demand and for net load.

What the figure and table show. PACE spends about 34 hours a year within 5 % of its peak (median of 2019–2024; 21–40 across years), spread over about 12 days, and only 11 hours on a net-load basis. ERCO's peak is far broader (95 hours). A single "top-k hours" rule would therefore mean very different things in different BAs, which is why rush-hour definitions are per BA and percentile-based, with bootstrap intervals for the year-to-year noise.

The heatmaps below place each year's 100 highest-demand hours on a month × local-hour grid (2019–2024 pooled; darker = more hours). PACE's sit entirely in June–September, mostly 16:00–21:00 local.

4. The BA's own forecast as a baseline¶

What the DF is. Each BA files a day-ahead demand forecast for every hour of the next day. EIA publishes the forecast for day D at about 11:00 ET on day D (EIA-930 About page), and in our snapshot the DF ran past the last reported demand hour (§1.2). So the DF is not available at a day-ahead issue time on D−1. It is a baseline to beat, never an input.

Alignment. A forecast published one hour off would look worse than it is. We shift the DF by −1, 0 and +1 hours against reported demand and compute the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) per calendar year, using only scored hours (not imputed, not spikes). The lowest line is the best alignment.

In [16]:
base = (pre.filter(pl.col("ba").is_in(["PACE", "PJM", "CISO"]) & ~pl.col("demand_imputed") & ~pl.col("d_spike"))
        .select("ba", "ts_utc", "year", "demand_mw", "demand_forecast_mw"))
parts = []
for k in (-1, 0, 1):
    shifted = base.select("ba", (pl.col("ts_utc") + pl.duration(hours=k)).alias("ts_utc"),
                          pl.col("demand_forecast_mw").alias("df_k"))
    j = base.join(shifted, on=["ba", "ts_utc"]).filter((pl.col("df_k") > 0) & (pl.col("demand_mw") > 0))
    parts.append(j.group_by("ba", "year").agg(
        ((pl.col("df_k") - pl.col("demand_mw")).abs() / pl.col("demand_mw")).mean().mul(100).alias("mape"))
        .with_columns(pl.lit(k).alias("shift_h")))
align = pl.concat(parts).sort("ba", "year", "shift_h")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.2), sharex=True)
for ax, ba in zip(axes, ["PACE", "PJM", "CISO"]):
    for k, color in ((-1, "#8a8984"), (0, "#2a78d6"), (1, "#eb6834")):
        a = align.filter((pl.col("ba") == ba) & (pl.col("shift_h") == k)).sort("year")
        ax.plot(a["year"], a["mape"], marker="o", ms=3, color=color, label=f"DF shifted {k:+d} h")
    ax.set_title(ba)
    ax.set_xlabel("Calendar year (2025 = Jan-Oct)")
    ax.set_ylim(0, 12)
axes[0].set_ylabel("MAPE vs reported demand (%)")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle("Is the BA's day-ahead forecast aligned? Lower is better (scored hours only)", x=0.01, ha="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
(align.with_columns(pl.col("mape").round(2), pl.format("shift {}h", "shift_h").alias("shift"))
 .pivot(on="shift", index=["ba", "year"], values="mape").sort("ba", "year"))

What the figure shows. For PACE, the unshifted forecast (blue) is best every year: it is aligned. For PJM, shifting by +1 hour (orange) is better in every year, so PJM's DF is published one hour early. CISO matches PJM from 2022 on. (CISO's 2019 forecast is broken and off the chart.) Which series carries the offset cannot be told from EIA-930 alone (grid.md, open question 1). The rule: align per BA on the validation year only, and say so wherever the DF is shown.

The figure below is the profile's view of every BA: bars are validation-year MAPE (orange = candidate BAs), dots are the 2019–2024 calendar years.

What the table shows. On the validation year, the DF is a strong, stable baseline for SOCO (1.2 %), BPAT (2.0 %), ERCO and MISO (2.3 %). PACE sits at 4.0 % and over-forecasts (bias +2.7 %); it picks the day's peak hour within ±1 h on only about 71 % of days, so peak timing is where a better forecast could add value. Several DFs degraded in 2025 (AZPS, NEVP, SWPP, PACW): beating them is easy and must never be headlined without saying so.

5. Recommended BAs¶

The table pulls together the numbers behind the region choice: data completeness, the DF baseline, how dirty the grid is on average (production-based carbon intensity, modeled from fuel mix × EIA emission factors; see notebook 05), how much a 1-hour job could cut by waiting up to 24 h (perfect foresight), and how narrow the rush hour is.

Why these ten. PACE is the hero: complete data, the dirtiest grid in the set (45 % coal), a narrow summer rush hour and a beatable BA forecast. CISO, BPAT, NEVP and AZPS are the West's contrasts and PACE's trading partners or neighbours; PSCO is the Rocky Mountain peer; ERCO, SWPP, MISO and PJM cover the big markets, including the flat-carbon grids where waiting does not pay (PJM: 8 %). IPCO (PACE's largest export partner) and NYIS (rush hour = dirtiest hours) are optional.

Why not the others. PACW's DF degraded to 11.5 % and its gas generation reads zero for half the year; FPL lost 6.3 % of its 2022 demand hours; TVA, DUK, SOCO and ISNE have good data but flat carbon (9–14 % room) that duplicates PJM and MISO. WACM and WAUW retire inside the test window (§1.2).

Decisions this supports¶

From the decision log:

  • D-002: Utah's PACE is the hero region (complete data, narrow rush hour, beatable BA forecast; §1, §3, §4).
  • D-006: profile the data before the design, with the test window sealed (§0, §1.2).
  • D-019: PACE first, with a ~10-BA overview (§5).
  • D-020: the test window ends at the snapshot's availability cutoff (§1.2: 8,592 hours to 2026-10-25, DF published ahead of demand).
  • D-022: hour-beginning UTC everywhere; local time from one zone per BA (§0, §3).
  • D-023: forecast adjusted demand with spikes and values ≤ 0 removed; never score imputed hours (§2).
  • D-024: the BA's forecast is a baseline only, aligned per BA on validation (§4).
  • D-031: rush hour defined per BA by percentile; forecast demand and net load (§3).
  • D-032: the core region set, with WACM and WAUW left out (§1.2, §5).
